newsitem.title: UK: Britain's CWS looks for ways to secure its future.
newsitem.headline: Britain's CWS looks for ways to secure its future.

text.p: Britain's mutually owned Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) will discuss ways of protecting itself at its annual meeting on Saturday, after its recent battle to fend of a takeover attempt.
Delegates at the meeting will vote on a resolution urging the CWS board "to take all necessary steps to ensure the Society's assets are secured for current and future members".

It was proposed by a regional CWS committee during the unsuccessful 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) takeover bid by entrepreneur Andrew Regan. This collapsed last month when the CWS succeeded in blocking the audacious but now discredited takeover attempt through the courts and a key financial backer for Galileo, Regan's special bidding vehicle, withdrew its support.

But while Regan and his Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica failed to win the supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group, the affair has thrown the spotlight on the performance of the CWS and raised questions about its future.

The intense interest shown by City financiers and publicly quoted companies in the CWS - which traces its origins to 1844 when a group of artisans called the "Rochdale Pioneers" banded together in Lancashire, north west England - has not faded.
The Manchester-based group now supplies most of Britain's co-operative retail societies with everything from babyfood to coffins, truly encapsulating the idea of "cradle to grave".
But the group has lagged behind its competitors on the High Street and this has led to suggestions that its real value would be best unlocked by selling off its component parts.
These include the profitable Co-operative Bank, the Co-operative Insurance Society (CIS), opticians, travel agents, farms and the funeral business.
Having defeated Regan, who was supported in his break-up by a now dismissed CWS senior manager, the CWS management faces the task of modernising the movement and avoiding another attempt to buy it.
"It is certainly in play. The only real way to stop a repeat (of the Regan attempt) is for there to be legislation," one Co-op insider told Reuters.
Such legislation looks a more likely prospect following the election on May 1 of the first Labour government in more than 18 years.
Labour is historically supportive of the co-operative movement and after its recent landslide victory has 26 Co-op sponsored members of parliament.
These individuals are likely to pressure the new government to consider seriously a parliamentary bill put forward by the UK Co-operatives Council giving co-operatives a separate legal identity.
The council represents all forms of co-operation, including credit unions, agricultural co-operative and housing co-ops.

"The law badly needs updating," Geoff Simpson, assistant to the chief executive of the council, told Reuters on Friday. "It is not designed to stop changes being made but will put them (the co-operatives) in a modern context," he added.
Helen Liddell, the new Economic Secretary to the Treasury, has been presented with the draft bill and Simpson said that while there is no guarantee that the government will accept it, he is hopeful.
Proponents of the move are quick to point out that it was not drafted hastily in response to Regan's CWS approach but has in fact been in the pipeline since 1991.

More immediately, however, the CWS and its chief executive Graham Melmoth, must convince its varied membership that it has embarked on the right course to steer it successfully into the next millennium.

With at least one action group calling for greater accountability to individual members and efficiency through reform of the democratic structure, decentralisation and working with the private sector, it will have its work cut out.

But if tradition is to be maintained, members are likely to be glancing anxiously at their watches as the 1400 GMT kick-off time for the English FA cup soccer final looms rather than concentrating on the future of the business.

"There's always an effort to get the meeting over in good time, but there's always something on the agenda which keeps it going until half-time," said one veteran of the Co-op meetings. ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
